title: Rolling Out a Design
summary: Getting a new design live safely with phased rollout, feature flags, and shadow traffic — and having a real rollback plan before you ship, not after something breaks.

slides.markdown:
Shipping a design isn't a single deploy — it's a controlled sequence of steps that each let you catch a problem before it reaches every user. A **rollout strategy** is how you get from "the code is merged" to "100% of traffic runs the new path" without betting the whole system on day one.

The strategies here — phased ramps, feature flags, shadow traffic — aren't optional polish; treat rollout as part of the design itself, decided before launch, not improvised after something breaks.

slides.sectionTitle: Why the rollout is part of the design, not an afterthought
slides.markdown:
It's tempting to treat "how we ship it" as a deployment detail separate from "what we're building." That framing hides real design decisions: can this change be turned off instantly if it misbehaves? Can it run at 1% of traffic without corrupting data for the other 99%? Those aren't operational afterthoughts — they constrain the design itself.

A design that can only be deployed all-at-once, with no partial state, is a riskier design even if the end state is identical to one that supports gradual rollout. Two teams can build the functionally same feature; the one that designed for a phased rollout from the start ships with far less risk.

The practical implication: when you're proposing a design, propose the rollout plan alongside it — not as a follow-up.

slides.sectionTitle: Phased rollout: percentage ramps and the metrics that gate each step
slides.markdown:
A **phased rollout** exposes the new path to a growing percentage of traffic — 1%, then 5%, then 25%, then 100% — with a pause at each step to check that nothing regressed before moving to the next. The percentage schedule matters less than what gates each step forward.

Define the gating metrics *before* you start: error rate, p99 latency, a business metric like checkout completion — with explicit thresholds, not "it looks fine." "It looks fine" is not a threshold; a 0.3% jump in error rate can be invisible in a dashboard glance but very real in aggregate at 25% of traffic.

A phase should stay live long enough to catch issues that only show up on a delay — a memory leak, a slow cache-warming effect, a weekly traffic pattern — not just long enough for the on-call engineer to eyeball a graph for five minutes.

slides.sectionTitle: Feature flags as a design tool: decoupling deploy from release
slides.markdown:
A **feature flag** is a runtime switch that decides whether a code path is active, without requiring a new deploy to change it. Its real value in a rollout is decoupling *deploy* (the code is on production machines) from *release* (users are actually experiencing it) — you can deploy dark, then release gradually, then instantly disable if something's wrong, all without touching the deploy pipeline.

This is strictly faster than rollback-via-redeploy: flipping a flag is seconds; reverting a deploy is minutes to tens of minutes, plus the risk of the rollback deploy itself failing.

The cost: flags accumulate. A flag left in code six months after full rollout is dead weight and a source of confusing branches — treat flag removal as part of the rollout's definition of done, not a someday cleanup task.

slides.sectionTitle: Shadow traffic and dark launches: testing the real path without real consequences
slides.markdown:
**Shadow traffic** copies real production requests to the new path in parallel, comparing its output against the current system's, without ever returning the new path's result to the user — so you find out how the new code behaves under real traffic patterns with zero user-facing risk. A **dark launch** is closely related: the new path runs live, sometimes even user-facing on the backend, but is hidden from users at the UI layer until it's proven out.

Shadow traffic is especially good at catching a class of bug phased rollout misses: a subtle output difference that doesn't show up as an error or a latency spike — the new recommendation engine returns technically-valid but wrong results, for instance — because nothing about the request fails, it just answers differently.

The limitation: shadow traffic can't safely test anything with a side effect (a payment, a write, a notification), since "compare without consequences" requires the new path to be read-only or fully sandboxed for the duration of the shadow period.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a rollout plan as a decision tree with abort points
slides.markdown:
![Rollout stages 1% to 100%, each checking gating metrics, with every stage able to branch off to a shared Abort box](assets/rollout-decision-tree.svg)

The useful mental model for a rollout isn't a straight line to 100% — it's a tree where every stage has an abort branch back to a known-safe state. Drawing it this way forces you to answer, for each stage, "what exactly happens if this fails here?" before you're actually in that situation.

If you can't name the abort action for a given stage, that stage isn't ready to ship — the plan is incomplete, not just the diagram.

slides.sectionTitle: Writing a rollback plan before launch, not during the incident
slides.markdown:
A **rollback plan** written during an incident is written by a stressed engineer under time pressure, often discovering for the first time that rollback isn't actually simple — maybe the new schema already has writes that the old code can't read, maybe the flag flip doesn't fully revert in-flight requests.

Writing it before launch forces you to answer the hard question while calm: is this change actually reversible? A pure feature-flag-gated code change usually is. A schema migration that's already dropped an old column is not — rollback there might mean restoring from backup, which has its own blast radius.

The plan should be a short, literal runbook: the exact commands or flag names, who's authorized to pull the trigger, and what "back to normal" looks like on a dashboard — not a vague "we'll revert if needed."

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: canary release vs blue-green vs shadow traffic — what each actually protects against
slides.markdown:
| | Canary release | Blue-green deployment | Shadow traffic |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Small % of real traffic hits the new version | Two full environments; traffic switches entirely from one to the other | Real requests are copied to the new path; response is discarded |
| Protects against | Bugs that show up under real traffic at small scale | A bad deploy — instant full rollback by switching back | Output-correctness bugs with no error signal |
| User impact if wrong | Limited to the canary percentage | None if caught before switch; full if caught after | None — the new path's output is never returned |
| Doesn't catch | Silent wrong-output bugs (no error, just wrong answer) | Gradual issues that only appear at full scale | Anything with a side effect (writes, payments) |

**How to decide:** canary and shadow traffic are complementary, not competing — use shadow traffic first to validate correctness with zero risk, then canary to validate behavior under real user impact at small scale. Blue-green is more about deploy safety than about behavior validation.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a rollout with no kill switch because "it should be fine"
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We tested this thoroughly in staging — we don't need a kill switch, just deploy it."

**Why it's wrong:** staging traffic never fully matches production — the data shapes, the concurrency, the edge cases from real users are different by definition. "Thoroughly tested" reduces the odds of a problem; it doesn't make a kill switch unnecessary, and the two aren't substitutes for each other. When something does go wrong at 2am with no flag to flip, the only option is an emergency redeploy under pressure — exactly the slow, risky path a kill switch exists to avoid.

**Correct model:** every rollout ships with an instant, no-deploy-required way to turn the new behavior off, regardless of how confident the team is going in — confidence and a kill switch address different failure scenarios, not the same one.
